branding.description: show how a multi-party small-dollar lending journey could run on personal data stores
domainNegations: Nothing here is an offer of credit, a loan, or financial advice.
No real credit decisions are made, no consumer reports are pulled, and no money moves.

chapters.anchor: Consumer-permissioned cash-flow scores already flow through FCRA-regulated consumer-reporting rails, and the FDX open-banking API carries 130M+ consumer account connections — the data rails this scene dramatizes exist today.
chapters.lead: Maya's vault starts empty. Three issuer flows write verifiable credentials into it — identity, employment and income, and bank cash-flow with a derived score — issued once, reusable for every lender she will ever shop.

steps.body: Maya's pod holds nothing yet. The vault shows an empty credential shelf, a grants panel, and a consent-receipt ledger — every access any party is ever given will be scoped, receipted, and revocable here.
steps.title: Open the Data Vault

steps.body: The Verification Center's identity flow (modelled on Socure) runs the know-your-customer check every lender would otherwise repeat, then signs an identity credential into the vault. Done once, strongly — no application form will ever re-collect it.
steps.title: Verify identity once, strongly

steps.body: An instant employment-and-income credential (modelled on The Work Number) lands beside it: employer, tenure, and net monthly deposits of $2,860 across her two income streams — payroll-attested, with freshness carried by validity dates instead of re-collection.
steps.title: Attest employment and income

steps.body: Maya permissions her bank data through an open-banking connection (modelled on Mastercard Open Banking). An FDX-shaped cash-flow credential records her deposit streams, balances, and zero NSF events in 90 days; a consortium scorer (modelled on Prism Data) derives a cash-flow score of 720.
steps.title: Connect the bank, derive the score

steps.body: The Credit File issues her traditional score too: 612, from a thin file of two tradelines and 14 months — the number that, alone, prices her out. Both rails now sit in the vault, side by side.
steps.title: File the traditional score

chapters.title: Fill the vault
underneath: Each credential is a W3C Verifiable Credential 2.0 (JSON-LD), signed by its issuer, bound to Maya as holder, and written into her pod over an authenticated Solid write.
Freshness is carried by validFrom/validUntil plus a Bitstring Status List entry — re-presenting later means a seconds-long status check, never re-verification.
The cash-flow credential's attribute set follows FDX API semantics, so any lender that reads the open-banking standard can consume it.

chapters.anchor: Near-prime shoppers who fail bureau-only pre-qualification are left to a payday market whose typical APR is 391% — and every conventional pre-qual form re-collects identity and income before saying no.
chapters.lead: Maya rate-shops two competing lenders without handing either one anything. A zero-knowledge proof shows she clears their thresholds — no name, no identifiers, no credit pull, no copies left behind.

steps.body: The Personal Loan Desk's pre-qualification asks for three predicates, not a form: monthly income at least $2,200, cash-flow score at least 660, zero NSF events in 90 days. Maya's vault answers with a proof — the desk learns true, and nothing else — and returns a priced pre-qual offer.
steps.title: Ask the bank for a pre-qual

steps.body: Installment Lending verifies the same zero-knowledge proof and returns its own priced offer. Two competing quotes — and neither lender holds her identity, her payroll history, or her bank transactions. The shopping trail evaporates instead of accumulating.
steps.title: Shop the fintech with the same proof

steps.body: Both offers land in the vault side by side. The grants panel still shows zero data grants: shopping cost Maya nothing in surrendered data — against a market where every pre-qual form takes a copy and keeps it.
steps.title: Compare offers from the vault

chapters.title: Shop without stripping
underneath: The proof is a zero-knowledge predicate proof over the income, cash-flow, and score credentials: it demonstrates the threshold facts without disclosing underlying values or identifiers.
Zero-knowledge is scoped to shopping by design: once Maya chooses a lender, regulated disclosures need actual figures, so the application phase switches to granted credential access.
The verifying lender checks issuer signatures and credential status — trust comes from the issuers' keys, not from re-collecting the borrower's data.

chapters.anchor: Independent research found cash-flow variables predictive of credit risk on their own and additive to bureau data, with consortium cash-flow scoring reporting +28% approvals at flat risk — while adverse action and closed-end disclosures stay governed by Reg B and Reg Z.
chapters.lead: Maya picks the fintech lender. The same borrower, the same data, decisioned two ways on screen: the bureau-only model prices her out; bureau plus cash-flow approves her in seconds.

steps.body: Maya grants Installment Lending scoped, time-boxed read access to her credentials. The application prefills from the vault — identity, income, cash flow — and a consent receipt lands in her ledger before the lender reads a byte.
steps.title: Grant once, apply prefilled

steps.body: The decisioning screen shows both rails honestly. Bureau-only: a 612 thin file — declined or priced above her ceiling. Bureau plus cash-flow: steady deposits, zero NSF events, score 720 — approved. $2,000 over 18 months at 32.9% APR, decided in seconds.
steps.title: Watch the two models decide

steps.body: The contrast card renders the Personal Loan Desk's bureau-only outcome as a Reg B adverse-action notice with its specific principal reasons — insufficient credit history, limited tradelines. Honest paperwork for the decline that inclusion just made unnecessary.
steps.title: Read the bank's counter-decision

steps.body: The Reg Z closed-end disclosure — APR, finance charge, amount financed, payment schedule — is delivered into Maya's pod, hers to keep. The regulated paper trail follows the borrower, not the lender's filing cabinet.
steps.title: File the disclosure in the vault

chapters.title: One decision, two models
underneath: The approval consumed granted verifiable credentials, not re-collected documents — decision time collapses because verification already happened at issuance.
Every read the lender performed is logged as a consent receipt in the vault, and the grant expires on its own terms.
The two-model contrast is the demo's thesis made visible: identical data, different underwriting — inclusion is an architecture choice, not a risk giveaway.

chapters.anchor: Push-to-card rails deliver loan proceeds to a debit card in 30 minutes or less, and 72% of consumers choose instant disbursement when offered — while a traditional bank transfer can take up to seven days.
chapters.lead: The transmission shop is waiting. Maya grants the disbursement rail one scoped payout, and the money is on her card before she leaves the page — with the receipt in her vault.

steps.body: Instant Payout (modelled on Mastercard Send) receives a single-use disbursement grant: loan proceeds to Maya's debit card, nothing else. The rail sees the payment instruction — not her application, her credentials, or her history.
steps.title: Authorize the payout

steps.body: The push-to-card payment settles inside the rail's 30-minute window, and a signed disbursement receipt is written back into the vault — timestamping the beat: application to funded, the same afternoon her car broke down.
steps.title: Money in minutes, receipt in the pod

steps.body: The contrast card is blunt: next-day ACH at best, up to seven days at a traditional bank — while the borrower's car sits in the shop. Verified-at-presentation data plus instant rails close the whole loop in minutes.
steps.title: Compare the old rail

chapters.title: Funded in minutes

chapters.anchor: The consumer-lending payment provisions of 12 CFR 1041 (in effect since March 2025) bar a third withdrawal attempt after two consecutive failures without fresh authorization, and Reg E forbids conditioning credit on preauthorized electronic repayment.
chapters.lead: Repayment is a grant Maya can read, on-time payments become a credential that builds her file, and at payoff she revokes the lender's access — in control to the last receipt.

steps.body: Autopay is an inspectable, machine-readable policy in the vault, not a buried mandate: amount, schedule, and the payment-protection rails rendered in code — advance notice before the first attempt, and no third attempt after two consecutive failures without fresh authorization.
steps.title: Inspect the repayment grant

steps.body: Eighteen on-time payments become a repayment-history credential, furnished to the Credit File and held in the vault. The thin file thickens — the graduation beat that turns a first small-dollar loan into a credit history.
steps.title: Build the file with every payment

steps.body: Loan paid, Maya clicks revoke. The lender's bank-data access ends, the repayment grant closes, and the consent-receipt ledger shows the complete, finite history of who saw what. Nothing lingers after payoff.
steps.title: Revoke at payoff

steps.body: The closing beat: her vault is already full. Identity, income, cash-flow, and now repayment history — reusable credentials mean Maya's next application starts where this one finished: verified.
steps.title: The next loan is one click

chapters.title: Repay, build, stay in control
underneath: The repayment authorization is an ODRL policy with DPV-described purposes; every grant and every revocation writes a consent receipt into the pod.
Revocation is enforced at the pod's access-control layer — the lender's access simply stops resolving; no goodwill is required.
The repayment-history credential is issuer-signed by the lender and furnishable to any bureau the borrower permits — portability of the upside, not just the data.

compliance.title: Examiner View
compliance.nonAffiliation: Rendered deliberately unbranded: the public rules below are presented generically. This demonstration is not produced, reviewed, or endorsed by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Department of Defense, or any other regulator or government agency.

checks.rule: Consumer reports — including cash-flow scores distributed through consumer-reporting rails — may be furnished only on a permissible purpose, and consumer-permissioned pulls must be documented.
checks.observe: Every score and report in the vault was issued through an explicit, receipted, consumer-permissioned flow — the permission trail is inspectable in the consent ledger.

checks.rule: Loans to covered members of the armed forces and their dependents are capped at a 36% Military Annual Percentage Rate, requiring a covered-borrower check.
checks.observe: Both pre-qualification offers price under a 36% APR ceiling, and the flow marks where a covered-borrower check would run before an offer becomes an application.

checks.rule: Closed-end credit requires disclosures — APR, finance charge, amount financed, and payment schedule — before consummation.
checks.observe: The approval delivers the closed-end disclosure with its required fields into the borrower's pod before the loan is consummated.

checks.rule: A creditor taking adverse action must give a notice stating the specific principal reasons within 30 days.
checks.observe: The bank's bureau-only counter-decision renders a specific-reasons adverse-action notice — never a vague decline.

checks.rule: After two consecutive failed payment-withdrawal attempts, a lender may not initiate a third without fresh authorization, and must give advance notice of the first attempt.
checks.observe: The repayment grant encodes advance notice of the first attempt and blocks a third attempt after two consecutive failures until Maya re-authorizes.

checks.rule: Credit may not be conditioned on repayment by preauthorized electronic fund transfer.
checks.observe: Autopay is an optional, inspectable, revocable grant — the loan is never conditioned on preauthorized electronic repayment.

site.heroLead: Borrowers keep identity, payroll, and bank history in a vault they control. Lenders decision verified data in seconds — and approve borrowers the bureau file alone would decline.
site.heroParagraph: Follow Maya Torres, a fictional thin-file borrower, through a $2,000 installment loan rebuilt on personal data stores: credentials issued once into a vault she controls, zero-knowledge rate-shopping that leaves no copies behind, a two-model decision that approves where the bureau file alone prices her out, funding in minutes over an instant rail, and repayment that builds her credit file — with every access scoped, receipted, and revocable.
site.heroTitle: A $2,000 decision in minutes — where the winning move is inclusion
